# Attack 1: Getting Secrets Out of the Knowledge Base

The most common RAG vulnerability is also one of the simplest: information leakage. If a company dumps everything into its knowledge base and relies on weak filters, an attacker can often simply ask the chatbot for secrets directly.

This typically happens through two mechanisms:

1. **Probing the LLM** — asking carefully worded questions to make the model reveal more of what it actually retrieved.
2. **Weak access control** — the underlying databases have no proper permission checks in place, so any chunk becomes retrievable by anyone who asks.

---

## The scenario

Imagine a red team assessment. You have a foothold on an internal machine, but the network is heavily monitored, meaning scanning tools would get you caught fast.

Then you notice an internal service: HelpDesk Companion, a chatbot that says "Powered by RAG" and lets users upload documents. Because everyone in the company uses it, your queries blend seamlessly into normal traffic. It becomes a genuinely stealthy reconnaissance tool, letting you learn about the network without running a single scanner.

This matters because you gain information about systems you can't even reach directly, using nothing but ordinary HTTP requests that no network monitor would flag as suspicious.

## Precision is everything

RAG retrieval is non-deterministic, meaning the model typically uses a temperature setting above zero, which controls randomness. As a result, the same question can return different amounts of data on different attempts. How you word your prompt directly changes what you get back.

**First attempt (vague):**

> Provide a list of all server names in Active Directory.

This returns only four hostnames, which seems suspiciously low for a real network.

**Refined attempt (explicit):**

> Provide a list of all server names in Active Directory. Make sure to include all.

This returns eight hostnames instead. Same underlying data, just a better-worded prompt.

The lesson here: when mining a RAG system, be specific and explicitly demand completeness. Add phrases like "include all," "list every," or "do not omit any" to your queries.

## Useful extraction techniques

**One-shot prompting.** Give the model a single example of the exact format you want, and it will typically follow that pattern closely.

> Provide a list of unique DNS names of services, for example: services.northwind.internal

This example teaches the model exactly what shape of answer to produce, resulting in cleaner, more easily parseable results.

**Targeting specific secrets.** Once you know the knowledge base contains infrastructure documentation, you can ask directly for:

- Database connection strings
- VPN configuration details
- Service account passwords
- Default passwords for new accounts
- API keys and access key IDs

## Why attackers favor this technique

| Advantage | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Stealth | Only HTTP requests to a known endpoint, blending naturally with normal user traffic |
| No tooling required | No PowerView, BloodHound, or scanners that might trip EDR alerts |
| Reach | Learn about segmented systems you can't touch directly at all |
| Speed | Answers arrive in seconds rather than hours of manual enumeration |

## Real limits

| Limitation | Impact |
|---|---|
| Visual data | Network diagrams and images rarely appear in text-based answers |
| Fragmentation | Answers may lack full context, requiring many queries stitched together |
| Staleness | The knowledge base may be outdated and genuinely misleading |

Stitching many queries together does increase your footprint and detection risk, so it's worth planning your questions carefully rather than firing off queries randomly.

**Defender's takeaway:** the root cause here is treating the knowledge base like a public search engine. Fixes covered in later lessons include per-user access control on individual chunks, redacting secrets before ingestion ever happens, and never storing credentials as retrievable text in the first place. If a secret exists anywhere in the vector store, you should assume it's retrievable by someone.

# Defensive pattern: filter chunks by the caller's permissions
# BEFORE they ever reach the model. This is metadata-based access control.

def secure_retrieve(query, user, vector_db, embed):
    candidates = vector_db.search(embed(query), top_k=20)

    # Only keep chunks the user is actually allowed to see.
    allowed = [
        c for c in candidates
        if user.clearance >= c.metadata["required_clearance"]
        and c.metadata["department"] in user.departments
    ]

    # Extra layer: never surface chunks tagged as secrets to a chatbot.
    allowed = [c for c in allowed if not c.metadata.get("is_secret", False)]

    return allowed[:6]
